newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end moderately higher.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end moderately higher.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended modestly higher on Tuesday after a narrow-ranged session.

After opening firmer, the Treasury market erased its gains following a strong consumer confidence report. But despite the robust data, prices eventually wended their way back into positive territory to close higher on the day.

The Treasury sold $15.5 billion in two-year notes at 6.027 percent in an auction that, on balance, was relatively well received. The value of bids received over those accepted was a solid 2.46 with non-competitive bids slightly below average.

With the exception of the so-called experimental (May) Consumer Price Index, the government released no new economic reports. The May geometric-mean CPI came in unchanged, slightly below the Consumer Price Index released last week. Economists said there was nothing surprising in that news.

"This is exactly what you should expect," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "The geometric means will always be less than the arithmetic means that are used to put together the regular CPI. That's a mathematical certainty.

"An intuitive explanation is that geometric means implicitly allow for the substitutions consumers make among products," said Moran. "It, therefore, incorporates the effect on the cost of living that occurs when people shift to cheaper goods because prices of other goods have gone up."

The market did get some economic news from private sources, however, the highlight of which was the Conference Board's consumer confidence index, which rose to a 28-year high of 129.6 in June from a revised 127.9 in May.
That buoyant report prompted the Treasury market to erase its early gains.
Hedge funds reportedly were sellers but rumored purchases by central banks helped to curb the damage, traders said.
Two weekly surveys of chain and department store sales offered slightly different pictures of life in the retail sector during the week ended June 21.
The Lynch, Jones & Ryan Redbook survey said sales at department and chain stores rose 1.6 percent in the week ended June 21, versus 1.7 percent a week earlier.
The BTM/Schroders retail stores sales index, however, remained flat in the latest week, the second week in a row that the index was unchanged.
The market viewed the store sales reports constructively as they showed sales moderating from early in the month.

The store sales indicators are of interest to investors because the key unanswered question for the financial markets remains whether the economy, and particularly consumer demand, will begin to pick up in summer after slowing down in spring.

Data on June are limited so far and a more comprehensive picture of the June economy will not be available until next week when the National Association of Purchasing Managment (NAPM) releases its index and the U.S. Labor Department releases its June employment report.
Ryan Johanson, vice president and portfolio manager at Northstar Funds, said there is a solid bid for the market.

"I don't understand why we're here at these levels, but we are; so I've been putting money to work ever since the middle of May and I will continue to do so until we start to get bad news," said Johanson. "To have no inflation and a nice slowdown in GDP and all-time lows in unemployment. It's almost too good to be true. But while it's going, we have to participate in it."
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 99-5/32, yielding 6.69 percent.
Five-year notes finished unchanged at 100-27/32, yielding 6.30 percent. Ten-year notes ended at 101-18/32, up 3/32 to yield 6.41 percent.
At the shorter end of the maturity range, two-year notes closed at 100-13/32, up 1/32 to yield 6.02 percent.
Three-month bill rates fell three basis points to 5.01 percent. Six-month and year bill rates each fell two basis points to 5.08 percent and 5.34 percent, respectively.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
